name: Iaai
catalog_quote: Tryon 1968:1: 'A Iai utterance containing no pauses and not more than one syllable bearing primary stress is a word.' 'In Iai, stress is non-phonemic. It is conditioned by the syllable and nuclear structure of the word.' '(a) Primary Stress. Primary stress always occurs on the first syllable of the word. (b) Secondary Stress. Secondary stress occurs on the final syllable of all tri-syllabic words…

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding Tryon 1968 passage is verbatim in the held at printed pp. 1-2 (PDF pp. 13-14), and the p. 2 examples (/émakàn/, /máhiñèn/, /húčučè/ = 101; /bárakòñɛn/ = 1010) match the catalog string stress placement coded per word length as 10 101 1010 10010 (1 = a stressed syllable); StressTyp2's own passage for the StressTyp2 entry for this language quotes the same rule, so the recorded StressTyp2 contradiction (100 vs 101) is StressTyp2's slip, not ours. (2) Deciding source is a 1968 primary descriptive grammar; the fuller reference grammar is Ozanne-Rivierre 1976 (not yet obtained, print only), but Lynch 2002:777, which abstracts O-R 1976 and which we hold, states the identical primary-initial / secondary-final-in-trisyllables / secondary-penult-otherwise rule, so two independent descriptive lines agree. Dotte 2013 (downloaded now, 529 pp) is silent on accent. (3) Nothing found suggests the classification is wrong; the record's grade field is empty, so the action is to upgrade the evi

sources.quote: "1. Stress — In Iai, stress is non-phonemic. It is conditioned by the syllable and nuclear structure of the word. There are three degrees of stress in Iai: primary stress, secondary stress and unstress. These three degrees of stress occur as follows: (a) Primary Stress — Primary stress always occurs on the first syllable of the word. sources.quote: 'Primary stress occurs on the initial syllable of a word, while secondary stress occurs on the final syllable of trisyllabic words and on the penultimate syllable of words of more than three syllables.' Sketch 'based mainly on Ozanne-Rivierre (1976), with some data from Tryon (1968b) and Ozanne-Rivierre (1984)' (p. 776).
